title: Explain the planning and scheduling of tasks in a production environment

lessons.title: Production planning and its levels
lessons.html:
What production planning is

Production planning means deciding in advance what must be produced, how much, when, where, with which people, machines and materials, and at what cost. On a farm it turns the owner's goals, such as 'deliver 400 tonnes of export citrus' or 'sell 1 200 weaners this year', into practical work.

Levels of planning

LevelTime spanWhoFarm example
Strategic (long-term)3 to 10 yearsOwner, top managementPlant 20 ha of new macadamias; build a new piggery
Tactical (medium-term)A season or a yearFarm managerCrop plan per block; breeding plan; budget; labour needs per month
Operational (short-term)A month, week or daySupervisor, team leaderWhich team sprays which block on Tuesday; milking roster; tractor allocation

The levels must fit together. A team leader's weekly plan carries out a part of the season plan, which supports the long-term strategy.

Inputs to a plan

  • Targets: quantity, quality and delivery dates from the market or buyer.
  • Resources: people and their skills, tractors and implements, land, water, inputs such as seed, fertiliser and feed.
  • Constraints: weather, rainfall and irrigation quotas, withdrawal periods and pre-harvest intervals on chemical labels, legal working hours, budget.
  • Information: records from previous seasons, soil and leaf analyses, production figures.

Why plan?

Without a plan, people wait for instructions, tractors stand idle while another block is late, inputs run out at the wrong time and deliveries are missed. A plan helps everyone work towards the same targets and makes it possible to measure progress.

lessons.title: Scheduling tasks
lessons.html:
From plan to schedule

A schedule puts tasks in order with dates, times and responsible people. Planning says what must be done; scheduling says exactly when and by whom.

Steps to build a schedule

  1. List the tasks. For example, for planting a maize block: soil sample, lime, plough, disc, plant, fertilise, weed control.
  2. Estimate the duration of each task from records and experience.
  3. Identify dependencies. Some tasks must finish before others start: you cannot plant before the land is prepared.
  4. Assign resources: people, tractors and implements, inputs.
  5. Check for clashes: the same tractor or team booked twice.
  6. Set dates and communicate the schedule to everyone involved.

Scheduling tools

  • Gantt chart: a bar chart showing each task against time. Easy to see overlaps and progress.
  • Weekly work board or roster: who does what each day, posted in the workshop or office.
  • Checklists and job cards: for each task, with targets and sign-off.
  • Farm management software or spreadsheets.

The critical path

The longest chain of dependent tasks decides the earliest finish date. This is the critical path. A delay on any task on the critical path delays the whole job. A supervisor watches these tasks most closely. For example, in a packhouse, late arrival of cartons delays packing, which delays loading the export container.

Scheduling people

Rosters must respect the Basic Conditions of Employment Act on working hours, overtime and rest periods. Spread skilled workers so every team has someone who can operate key equipment.

lessons.title: Optimising production
lessons.html:
What optimisation means

Production optimisation means getting the best output, in quantity and quality, from the resources you have, at the lowest reasonable cost, without harming safety or the environment.

Techniques a team leader can use

  • Remove bottlenecks. Find the slowest step and improve it. If the sorting table in the packhouse is slow, add a sorter or re-balance the line.
  • Balance the workload. Give teams similar amounts of work so no one waits.
  • Reduce waiting and travel time. Plan routes so a tractor works neighbouring blocks in sequence; have inputs ready at the field before the team arrives.
  • Batch similar work. Do all spraying of one product in one pass, rather than mixing several times.
  • Preventive maintenance. Service tractors and pumps on schedule to avoid breakdowns in the busy season.
  • Standard work methods. Train everyone in the best method for the job, for example the correct pruning cut, so quality is consistent.
  • Reduce waste. Waste includes rejected fruit, spilt feed, overuse of fertiliser, re-work and idle time.
  • Measure. Record output per worker, per hectare or per hour, and compare with targets.

Example

A harvest team of 20 picks 80 bins a day, but the tractor taking bins to the packhouse makes the team wait twice a day. Adding a second trailer so one is always in the orchard removes the waiting. If output rises to 90 bins a day, that is 10 more bins with the same labour.

lessons.title: Reviewing and commenting on plans
lessons.html:
Plans must be checked

A plan is only as good as its results. A team leader monitors progress and gives meaningful feedback so that the plan can be improved.

Monitoring

  • Compare actual against planned: hectares sprayed, bins picked, litres milked, piglets weaned.
  • Check quality as well as quantity.
  • Note delays and their causes: breakdowns, rain, absent workers, late deliveries.

Making meaningful comments

Useful feedback is specific, based on facts and suggests a solution.

Not usefulMeaningful
'The plan is bad.''Block 7 spraying fell two days behind because the only 2 000-litre sprayer was booked for blocks 3 and 7 on the same day.'
'We need more people.''Picking output dropped 15% on the days we had six absentees. A standby list of casual workers would protect the harvest schedule.'

When to raise issues

  • Before the work starts, if you see a problem in the plan, such as a clash or missing inputs.
  • During the work, as soon as a delay will affect other tasks.
  • After the work, in a review meeting, to improve the next plan.

Contingency planning

Good plans include a 'plan B' for likely problems: what to do on rain days, who covers for an absent tractor driver, where to get a spare pump.

Key points

  • Planning happens at strategic, tactical and operational levels that must fit together.
  • A schedule sets tasks in order with dates, durations, resources and responsible people.
  • Watch the critical path: delays there delay the whole job.
  • Optimise by removing bottlenecks, reducing waiting and waste, and maintaining equipment.
  • Give specific, fact-based feedback with suggested solutions.

quiz.question: A farm manager makes a crop plan and budget for the coming season. Which level of planning is this?

options.text: The tasks done by the manager
The longest chain of dependent tasks that sets the earliest finish date

quiz.question: Which tool shows each task as a bar against time?
A harvest team often waits for the tractor to return with an empty trailer. Which optimisation technique fits best?

options.text: Reduce waiting time, for example by adding a second trailer

quiz.question: Which comment on a plan is the most meaningful?

options.text: Spraying fell two days behind because the only sprayer was booked for two blocks on the same day
